title: Sharding
subtitle: Horizontal data partitioning across independent database nodes: Shard Keys, Routing, Resharding, and Cross-Shard Joins.
keyTakeaways: Sharding splits a massive database into independent, isolated physical instances (shards), each holding a subset of rows.
Shard key selection is a permanent architectural commitment: choosing a poor shard key causes uneven data distribution and hotspotting.
Sharding eliminates single-node hardware limits, but sacrifices cross-shard joins, distributed ACID transactions, and foreign key integrity.

sections.heading: Shard Key Selection and Routing Mechanics
sections.body: Sharding should be your last resort when scaling a database—only when write IOPS or storage volume exceeds the limits of the largest available vertical hardware. Once you shard, selecting the shard key (partition key) dictates how traffic and storage distribute across the cluster.
bullets: Hash-Based Sharding: Computes `hash(shard_key) % num_shards`. Distributes rows uniformly across shards, but makes range queries (`WHERE created_at BETWEEN X AND Y`) scatter-gather across every single shard.

Range-Based Sharding: Partitions data by contiguous ranges (e.g., User IDs 1-1000 on Shard A, 1001-2000 on Shard B). Supports efficient range scans, but creates extreme hot shards if rows are inserted with auto-incrementing timestamps.
Directory-Based Sharding: Uses an external lookup table or consistent hashing ring to map entity IDs to shard locations, enabling flexible data migrations at the cost of an extra lookup hop.

sections.heading: Solving Cross-Shard Queries and Re-Sharding
sections.body: The operational cost of sharding emerges when business logic requires querying data stored across multiple physical shards.
bullets: Scatter-Gather Queries: If a query cannot filter by the shard key (e.g., `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_email = 'alice@example.com'` on an `order_id`-sharded database), the router must dispatch queries to all shards in parallel and merge results in memory.

Cross-Shard Joins: Traditional relational JOINs across shards are impossible. Applications must either denormalize data into the same shard, or query each shard independently and join in application memory.

Re-Sharding Complexity: When growing from 4 shards to 8 shards, modulo hashing (`hash % 4` to `hash % 8`) remaps ~75% of all keys. Using virtual bucket mapping (e.g., 1,024 fixed virtual buckets distributed across physical shards) ensures adding nodes only moves `1/N` keys.

tradeOffs.pros: Full ACID transactions; native relational JOINs; zero routing infrastructure; simple backups.
tradeOffs.cons: Hard physical limits on CPU, memory, and write IOPS; high cost at top cloud instance tiers.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Most systems handling under 20,000 writes/sec and under 5 TB of relational data.

tradeOffs.pros: Virtually unlimited storage and write throughput capacity; bounds the blast radius of single-node hardware failures.
tradeOffs.cons: Eliminates cross-shard ACID transactions; schema migrations require coordinating across dozens of nodes; complex resharding.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Hyperscale multi-tenant SaaS, global social networks, and payment engines processing 50k+ writes/sec.

interviewTip: In system design interviews, never jump straight to sharding without justifying it with numbers: 'A single AWS RDS Postgres instance can handle 20,000 writes per second. Because our peak write volume is 60,000 writes/sec, we are forced to shard. We will shard by `tenant_id` to ensure that 99% of queries remain single-shard operations.'
